agent_notes: The superscription 'of David' (לְדָוִד) is verse 1 in the Hebrew numbering (KJV 103:0), so it is glossed at pos 1 and given in both layers. The preposition lamed can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to' David; I kept the neutral 'Of David' in the literal layer.

בָּרֲכִי is an imperative feminine singular addressed to נַפְשִׁי (nefesh is grammatically feminine). STEPBible glosses 'O soul my' on the noun; I glossed the noun as 'my soul' and the verb as 'bless!'. In the second colon 'bless' is not repeated in the Hebrew; I put it in brackets, following Ibn Ezra, who reads the verb as doing double duty.

agent_notes: גָּמַל is the same root as גְּמוּלָיו in v. 2 ('benefits'). In v. 2 it is the good done; here it is repayment, which can be for ill. I repeat 'repay'/'repayments' in English to keep the echo visible; the dramatic layer plays on it too. The packet's STEPBible gloss puts 'to us' on both עָשָׂה לָנוּ and גָּמַל עָלֵינוּ.

Malbim's long astronomical reading (the daily and yearly motion of the sun, 365 days) is a medieval cosmological claim; I cite it for the 'east from west' asymmetry only in outline and leave the rest out of the commentary. Radak's explanation for why north and south are not used is given as his.

זָכוּר is a passive adjective ('remembered'), not an active participle. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David read it as 'remembered before him', that is, God keeps it in mind; the five English versions all make it active ('remembers'). I kept the passive in the literal layer and the active sense in the dramatic layer.

history.note: [consider] If the passive is meant, make the literal layer read something like '[it is] remembered that we [are] dust', to match the gloss. (PS.103.14: "זָ֝כ֗וּר כִּי־עָפָ֥ר אֲנָֽחְנוּ"; Ibn Ezra: "זכור הוא לפניו")

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses כִּי as 'if'; I read it as causal 'for', tying the verse to the grass and flower of v. 15 (so KJV, ASV, YLT, BBE all take it). The suffix on 'over him' (בּוֹ) and 'is not' (אֵינֶנּוּ) is masculine singular and has no stated antecedent: it can be 'the flower' (צִיץ) or the man himself. I kept the pronoun 'him/he' in the literal layer and let the commentary name both readings.

Several commentators (Radak, Metzudat David, Malbim, and the Targum's 'from this world to the world to come') read מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד־עוֹלָם as a statement about the afterlife. I treat that as a traditional reading and keep the plain sense 'from forever to forever'.

The Qere/Ketiv is not at issue here, but the verse repeats דבר twice (עֹשֵׂי דְבָרוֹ, בְּקוֹל דְּבָרוֹ). KJV and Webster render the first 'commandments' and the second 'word'; ASV and YLT keep 'word' twice. I repeat 'word'. Ibn Ezra's remark on the angels' reward and Meiri's identification of the angels with the 'separate intellects' are medieval readings I cite only as the commentators' views.

The eagle's renewal is explained in the commentaries by a molting or rebirth legend (Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David); I cite them as reports of what was said, not as natural history. The Radak and Meiri accounts of the eagle flying to the sphere of fire and plunging into the sea are medieval natural-philosophy, and I did not project them onto the psalmist.
